newsitem.title: USA: Capsule look at U.S. arms used against Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Capsule look at U.S. arms used against Iraq.

text.p: Here are capsule looks at U.S. military weapons used in Tuesday's cruise missile raid against military targets in southern Iraq.

Tomahawk Cruise Missiles: Unmanned 18-foot-long (5.6 metres) missiles weigh 2,650 pounds (1,193 kg) each and can be fired from both surface warships and submarines against targets up to 690 miles (1,104 km) away. A total of 13 of the accurate Tomahawks, which cost $1.2 million each, were fired on Tuesday. They contain computer map brains that allow them to follow pre-set course at earth-hugging altitude in any weather to target.

B-52 Bombers: Eight engine, Vietnam-era jets originally designed to drop nuclear bombs on former Soviet Union in world war that never came. They now carry advanced conventional air-to-ground (AGM) cruise missiles and bombs and can fly more than 7,500 miles (12,000 km) without refueling or around globe with help of refueling aircraft. Bombers used in raid were sent from Guam in western Pacific and refueled at British base on Diego Garcia Island in Indian Ocean.

AGM-86 Cruise Missiles: Unmanned little winged missiles are launched from B-52s and powered by turbofan jet engine that propels them at sub-sonic speeds of about 550 miles an hour (880 kph) like the sea-launched Tomahawks. "C" model of missile became operational in 1991 and was fired from B-52s at high-priority targets in Iraq early in 1991 Gulf War.

Advanced Aegis Cruiser Shiloh and Arleigh Burke Class Destroyer Laboon, both based in Persian Gulf, fired a total of 14 Tomahawks in Tuesday's raid. Shiloh is 567 feet (173 metres) long and carries crew of 364. Laboon is 466 feet (142 metres) long and carries crew of 323. They are among Navy's most sophisticated warships, designed to track and shoot down large numbers of attacking aircraft simultaneously as well as hunt submarines and surface ships ships.
